categories.name: Warm-ups
categories.blurb: Small, friendly problems for your first weeks. Loops, conditions, strings and lists.
pattern: Read the input carefully, decide what to return, then walk through the data once with a loop.
Most warm-ups are one loop plus one variable that accumulates the answer (a count, a sum, a best-so-far).

categories.name: Arrays & Hashing
categories.blurb: Trade memory for speed with sets and dictionaries.
pattern: When a brute-force answer compares every pair (O(n²)), ask: what would I need to remember to answer in one pass? Usually a set of things seen or a dict from value to index or count.
Hash lookups are O(1) on average, so one pass with a dict turns many O(n²) problems into O(n).
categories.template:
def one_pass(nums):
    seen = {}                 # value -> index (or count)
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if need(x) in seen:   # answer found using memory
            return seen[need(x)], i
        seen[x] = i
    return None

categories.name: Two Pointers
categories.blurb: Walk inward from both ends, or chase with a fast and slow pointer.
pattern: On sorted data (or symmetric problems like palindromes) put one pointer at each end. Compare, then move the pointer that can improve the answer.
Each step discards at least one element, so the scan is O(n) with O(1) extra memory.

categories.name: Sliding Window
categories.blurb: Grow a window on the right, shrink it on the left.
pattern: For 'longest/shortest contiguous subarray or substring such that…', keep a window [left, right]. Extend right one step at a time; while the window breaks the rule, move left forward.
Both pointers only move forward, so the total work is O(n) even though there is a loop inside a loop.

categories.name: Stack
categories.blurb: Last in, first out: matching brackets, undo, and monotonic stacks.
pattern: Use a stack when the most recent unfinished thing is the one you need next: an open bracket, an operand, a day waiting for a warmer day.
A monotonic stack keeps elements in increasing or decreasing order; each element is pushed and popped at most once, so it's O(n).

categories.name: Binary Search
categories.blurb: Halve the search space every step: O(log n).
pattern: If the data is sorted, or if the answer is monotonic (every value below some point fails and every value above passes), you can binary search it.
Keep an invariant about lo and hi and make sure each iteration shrinks the range, or you'll loop forever.

categories.name: Linked List
categories.blurb: Rewire pointers carefully; a dummy head saves edge cases.
pattern: Draw the boxes and arrows. Most bugs are a lost reference: save `nxt = cur.next` before you overwrite `cur.next`.
A dummy node before the head means you never special-case 'the head changed'. Fast/slow pointers find middles and cycles.
categories.template:
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev

categories.name: Trees
categories.blurb: Recursion is natural: solve for the children, combine at the parent.
pattern: Most tree problems are: what does each subtree return, and how does the parent combine the two answers? Write the base case for `None` first.
Use BFS with a queue when the problem says 'level' or 'closest'; use DFS (recursion) for everything else.

categories.name: Heaps
categories.blurb: Always know the smallest (or largest) item in O(log n).
pattern: A heap answers 'give me the current minimum' quickly while items keep arriving. For the top k of something, keep a min-heap of size k: the root is the k-th best.
Python's `heapq` is a min-heap; push negatives for a max-heap. In JavaScript there is no built-in heap, so sorting is fine at these sizes.

categories.name: Backtracking
categories.blurb: Explore every choice, undo it, try the next.
pattern: Build the answer one choice at a time. At each step: choose, recurse, un-choose. Record a copy when the partial answer is complete.
Prune early: if a partial answer can't possibly work, return before going deeper.

categories.name: Graphs
categories.blurb: Grids and networks: BFS, DFS and topological order.
pattern: Model the problem as nodes and edges. A grid is a graph where each cell links to its 4 neighbours.
BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS explores components; Kahn's algorithm (in-degree queue) orders tasks and detects cycles.

categories.name: Dynamic Programming
categories.blurb: Overlapping subproblems: solve each once, reuse forever.
pattern: Define the state in words ("dp[i] = the best answer for the first i items"), write the transition from smaller states, then the base cases.
Start with recursion plus memoisation if the table feels hard; convert to a bottom-up loop once it works.

categories.name: Greedy & Intervals
categories.blurb: Make the locally best choice, after sorting the right way.
pattern: Sort intervals by start (to merge) or by end (to schedule the most). Then one pass decides each interval by comparing with the last kept one.
A greedy choice needs a reason it's safe: an exchange argument that any optimal answer can be rearranged to include it.

categories.name: Math & Bits
categories.blurb: XOR tricks, counting bits and arithmetic insight.
pattern: `x ^ x == 0` and `x ^ 0 == x`, so XOR-ing everything cancels pairs. `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit.
Many 'find the missing/extra number' problems have an O(1)-memory answer with a sum formula or XOR.

categories.name: Design
categories.blurb: Build a data structure with guaranteed operation costs.
pattern: Pick the operations' target costs first, then combine structures that achieve them: a dict for O(1) lookup, a list or linked list for order, a second stack for running minimums.
Test with a sequence of operations, not single calls.

problems.title: FizzBuzz
desc: Given a whole number `n`, return a list of strings for the numbers 1 to `n`.
For multiples of 3 use `"Fizz"`, for multiples of 5 use `"Buzz"`, for multiples of both use `"FizzBuzz"`, and otherwise use the number itself as a string.
hints: Check the 'both' case first, or build the string by appending 'Fizz' and 'Buzz'.
`str(i)` in Python and `String(i)` in JavaScript turn a number into text.
editorial: Loop from 1 to n. A number divisible by 15 is divisible by both 3 and 5, so test that first (or build the word from two independent checks and fall back to the number if it's empty).
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output.

problems.title: Reverse a String
desc: Return the string `s` with its characters in reverse order.
Try writing it with a loop first, then look up the one-line idiom in your language.
hints: Start from the last index, `len(s) - 1`, and walk down to 0.
Python: `s[::-1]`. JavaScript: `[...s].reverse().join("")`.
editorial: Walk the indices from the end to the start and collect characters. Joining a list once is faster than adding to a string repeatedly, because strings are immutable and each `+` copies.

problems.title: Count the Vowels
desc: Return how many vowels (`a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u`, in upper or lower case) appear in the string `s`.
hints: Lower-case the string once so you only compare against five letters.
Membership in a string or set: `ch in "aeiou"`.
editorial: Convert to lower case, then count characters that are in the vowel set. One pass, constant extra memory.

solution.py:
def count_vowels(s):
    return sum(1 for ch in s.lower() if ch in "aeiou")

problems.title: Largest Number in a List
desc: Return the largest number in the non-empty list `nums` without using the built-in `max` (Python) or `Math.max` (JavaScript).
The point is to practise the 'best so far' pattern you'll use in hundreds of harder problems.
hints: Start with the first element as your best guess, not 0. Why would 0 be wrong?
Loop over the rest and replace the best when you see something bigger.
editorial: Initialise `best = nums[0]` (initialising to 0 fails when every number is negative). Walk the list once and update `best` whenever an element is larger.

problems.title: Sum of Digits
desc: Given a non-negative integer `n`, return the sum of its decimal digits.
Solve it with arithmetic (`%` and `//`) rather than converting to a string.
hints: `n % 10` is the last digit.
`n // 10` (Python) or `Math.floor(n / 10)` (JavaScript) drops the last digit.
editorial: Repeatedly take the last digit with `n % 10`, add it, then remove it by integer division by 10, until `n` is 0.
problems.complexity: O(d) time where d is the number of digits, O(1) space.

problems.title: Factorial
desc: Return `n!`, the product `1 × 2 × … × n`. By definition `0! = 1`.
Write it once with a loop and once with recursion. Which one would you trust for `n = 5000`?
constraints: 0 <= n <= 18 (so the answer fits in a JavaScript number exactly)
hints: Start the product at 1, not 0.
Recursive version: `n! = n × (n-1)!` with base case `0! = 1`.
editorial: A loop multiplying 1..n is the safest version. The recursive one is elegant but uses one stack frame per call, so very large `n` would exceed the recursion limit.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space for the loop.

problems.title: Is It a Leap Year?
desc: Return `true` if `year` is a leap year in the Gregorian calendar.
A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100, unless they are also divisible by 400. So 2000 was a leap year and 1900 was not.
hints: Combine the three rules with `and` / `or`.
`year % 400 == 0 or (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0)`
editorial: Translate the rule directly: divisible by 400, or divisible by 4 but not by 100. Order the checks from most specific to least to keep it readable.

solution.py:
def is_leap_year(year):
    return year % 400 == 0 or (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0)

problems.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
desc: Convert a temperature from degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit using `F = C × 9 / 5 + 32`.
hints: Translate the formula directly.
Multiply before dividing, or use 1.8.
editorial: A direct translation of the formula. -40 is the one temperature where both scales agree, which makes a nice sanity check.

solution.py:
def to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

problems.title: Count the Words
desc: Return how many words are in `sentence`. Words are separated by one or more spaces, and the sentence may start or end with spaces.
hints: Splitting on whitespace gives you the words.
In Python, `split()` with no argument ignores repeated spaces. In JavaScript, trim first and split on `/\s+/`.
editorial: Split on runs of whitespace and count the pieces. The edge case is an empty or all-space string, which has zero words (in JavaScript, `"".split(/\s+/)` gives `[""]`, so trim and check for empty first).

solution.py:
def count_words(sentence):
    return len(sentence.split())

args: a b c d e f

problems.title: Palindrome Number
desc: Return `true` if the integer `x` reads the same backwards as forwards. Negative numbers are never palindromes (the `-` is only at the front).
hints: Converting to a string is the quick way.
Without strings: build the reversed number with `% 10` and `// 10`.
editorial: Reverse the digits arithmetically (or compare the string with its reverse). Negative numbers fail immediately, and numbers ending in 0 can only be palindromes if they are 0.

problems.title: First Unique Character
desc: Return the index of the first character in `s` that appears exactly once, or `-1` if there is none.
hints: Count every character first.
Then scan again and return the first index whose count is 1.
editorial: Two passes: count characters with a dictionary, then find the first position whose character has count 1.

problems.title: Running Sum of an Array
desc: Return a list where element `i` is the sum of `nums[0]` through `nums[i]`.
hints: Keep a running total as you walk the list.
Append the total after adding each number.
editorial: Accumulate as you go. This **prefix sum** is a building block: with it, the sum of any range `i..j` is `prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]` in O(1).

problems.title: Max Consecutive Ones
desc: `nums` contains only 0s and 1s. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive 1s.
hints: Track the current run and the best run.
Reset the current run to 0 on a 0.
editorial: One pass with two counters: the current streak and the best streak seen.

problems.title: Plus One
desc: A non-negative integer is given as a list of its digits, most significant first. Add one and return the new list of digits.
constraints: No leading zeros except the number 0
hints: Work from the last digit backwards, like adding by hand.
A 9 becomes 0 and carries; if every digit carries, add a 1 in front.
editorial: Walk from the end: if the digit is less than 9, increment it and return. Otherwise set it to 0 and continue. If the loop finishes, the number was all 9s, so prepend 1.

problems.title: Two Sum
desc: Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`, as `[i, j]` with `i < j`.
Exactly one pair works, and you may not use the same element twice.
hints: The brute force checks every pair: O(n²). What do you need to remember to do one pass?
For each `x`, the partner you need is `target - x`. Have you seen it before?
editorial: Walk the list once with a dictionary from value to index. For each `nums[j]`, check whether `target - nums[j]` is already in the dictionary; if so, return its index and `j`. Otherwise store `nums[j]`. Checking before storing means an element never pairs with itself.

problems.title: Contains Duplicate
desc: Return `true` if any value appears at least twice in `nums`, and `false` if every element is distinct.
hints: A set remembers what you've seen with O(1) lookups.
Or compare `len(set(nums))` with `len(nums)`.
editorial: Add elements to a set; if an element is already there, you've found a duplicate. Sorting and comparing neighbours also works in O(n log n) with less memory.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
desc: Return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`: the same letters with the same counts, possibly in a different order.
constraints: s and t contain lowercase English letters
hints: Different lengths can never be anagrams.
Count letters of `s` up, letters of `t` down; every count must end at 0.
editorial: Build a frequency count for each string and compare. With only 26 letters, an array of 26 counters is enough and keeps memory constant.

problems.title: Majority Element
desc: Return the element that appears more than `n / 2` times in `nums`. It always exists.
Can you do it in O(1) extra memory?
hints: Counting with a dict works in O(n) memory.
Boyer–Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter; matching elements vote +1, others −1.
editorial: Boyer–Moore: when the counter hits 0, adopt the current element as the candidate. Each non-majority element can cancel at most one majority vote, and the majority has more than half, so it survives as the final candidate.

problems.title: Isomorphic Strings
desc: Two strings are isomorphic if the characters of `s` can be replaced to get `t`, where every occurrence of a character maps to the same character and no two characters map to the same one. Return whether `s` and `t` are isomorphic.
hints: One map is not enough: `ab` → `aa` must fail.
Keep a map in each direction, or compare the index of each character's first appearance.
editorial: Maintain `s→t` and `t→s` maps. For each pair, if either side already maps somewhere different, fail. Two maps enforce a one-to-one mapping.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space for a fixed alphabet.

problems.title: Intersection of Two Arrays
desc: Return the distinct values that appear in both `nums1` and `nums2`, in any order.
hints: Sets remove duplicates and test membership in O(1).
Set intersection: `&` in Python, a filter with `has` in JavaScript.
editorial: Turn one array into a set and keep the distinct values of the other that are in it.

solution.py:
def intersection(nums1, nums2):
    return list(set(nums1) & set(nums2))

problems.title: Group Anagrams
desc: Group the strings in `strs` so that anagrams are together. Return a list of groups; the order of groups and of words inside a group doesn't matter.
hints: Two words are anagrams exactly when their sorted letters are equal.
Use the sorted word as a dictionary key.
editorial: Map each word to a canonical key (its letters sorted, or a tuple of 26 counts) and append the word to `groups[key]`. The dictionary's values are the answer.
problems.complexity: O(n · k log k) time for n words of length up to k; O(n · k) space.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
desc: Return the `k` most frequent elements of `nums`, in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique.
hints: Count first. Then you need the k largest counts.
Bucket sort: a list where index `c` holds the values that appear `c` times.
editorial: Count with a dictionary. Then either sort the distinct values by count (O(n log n)), keep a min-heap of size k (O(n log k)), or use buckets indexed by count and read from the top (O(n)).
problems.complexity: O(n) time with buckets, O(n) space.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
desc: Return a list `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of every element of `nums` except `nums[i]`.
Do it in O(n) time without using division.
constraints: Every prefix and suffix product fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: answer[i] = (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i).
Fill the output left to right with prefix products, then sweep right to left multiplying in a running suffix product.
editorial: Two passes. First, `out[i]` = product of `nums[0..i-1]`. Then walk backwards with a running product of `nums[i+1..]`, multiplying it into `out[i]`. No division, so zeros need no special case.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space besides the output.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
desc: Given an unsorted list `nums`, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (like 4, 5, 6, 7) that can be formed from its elements.
Aim for O(n) time.
hints: Put everything in a set.
Only start counting from a number `x` when `x - 1` is not in the set: that's the start of a run.
editorial: Insert all numbers into a set. For each `x` that starts a run (no `x - 1` present), count up while `x + 1, x + 2, …` exist. Each number is visited by at most one run, so the total is O(n).

problems.title: Valid Sudoku
desc: Determine whether a partly filled 9 × 9 Sudoku `board` is valid: each row, each column and each of the nine 3 × 3 boxes must contain the digits 1–9 at most once. Empty cells are `"."`. The board doesn't need to be solvable.
hints: Keep a set for every row, every column and every box.
Box index for cell (r, c): (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3.
editorial: One pass over the 81 cells. For each digit, check and record it in its row set, column set and box set. A repeat anywhere means invalid.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
desc: Return the number of contiguous, non-empty subarrays of `nums` whose sum is exactly `k`. Numbers may be negative.
hints: A sliding window fails with negative numbers.
With prefix sums, sum(i..j) = prefix[j] − prefix[i−1]. Count how many earlier prefixes equal `prefix − k`.
editorial: Walk the array keeping a running prefix sum and a dictionary counting how often each prefix has occurred (starting with `{0: 1}`). At each step, every earlier prefix equal to `prefix - k` ends a subarray summing to `k` here.

problems.title: Rotate Image
desc: Rotate the `n × n` matrix 90 degrees clockwise **in place**. The judge inspects `matrix` after your function returns.
hints: Rotation = transpose (swap across the diagonal) then reverse each row.
Swap `m[i][j]` with `m[j][i]` only for `j > i`.
editorial: Transpose the matrix in place, then reverse every row. Both steps are in place, so no extra matrix is needed.

problems.title: Spiral Matrix
desc: Return all elements of the `m × n` matrix in spiral order: right along the top, down the right side, left along the bottom, up the left side, then inwards.
hints: Keep four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
After each side, move that boundary inwards; stop when they cross.
editorial: Shrink four boundaries as you peel off the outer ring. Guard the bottom row and left column with `top <= bottom` and `left <= right` checks so single rows or columns aren't visited twice.

problems.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
desc: If an element of `matrix` is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Do it **in place**; the judge inspects `matrix` afterwards.
hints: Don't zero things while scanning, or new zeros spread further.
Record which rows and columns contain a zero first, then apply.
editorial: First pass: collect the rows and columns that contain a zero. Second pass: zero every cell in those rows or columns. (The O(1)-space trick stores these markers in the first row and column.)
problems.complexity: O(m × n) time, O(m + n) space.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
desc: A phrase is a palindrome if, after lower-casing it and removing every non-alphanumeric character, it reads the same forwards and backwards.
Return `true` if `s` is a palindrome.
hints: Two pointers: one from each end, skipping characters that aren't letters or digits.
Python: `ch.isalnum()`. JavaScript: `/[a-z0-9]/i.test(ch)`.
editorial: Move `lo` right and `hi` left, skipping non-alphanumerics, and compare lower-cased characters. Stop at the first mismatch. No cleaned copy of the string is needed.

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
Was it a car or a cat I saw?
A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

problems.title: Move Zeroes
desc: Move every `0` in `nums` to the end while keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements.
Modify the list **in place**; the judge inspects `nums` after your function returns, so what you return is ignored.
hints: Keep a `write` index for where the next non-zero belongs.
After placing all non-zeros, fill the rest with zeros (or swap as you go).
editorial: Walk with a read pointer; each time you see a non-zero, swap it into position `write` and advance `write`. Non-zeros keep their order and zeros drift to the end.

problems.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
desc: `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain negatives. Return the squares of each number, also sorted, in O(n).
hints: The largest square is at one of the two ends.
Fill the output from the back with two pointers.
editorial: The biggest absolute value is always at an end of the sorted array. Compare the two ends, write the larger square at the back of the output, move that pointer inwards, repeat.

problems.title: Is Subsequence
desc: Return `true` if `s` is a subsequence of `t`: you can delete some (or no) characters of `t`, without reordering the rest, to get `s`.
hints: Walk through `t` once.
Advance a pointer in `s` each time its current character matches.
editorial: Greedy matching: scan `t`, and whenever the current character equals the next unmatched character of `s`, advance in `s`. If you match all of `s`, it's a subsequence.

problems.title: Two Sum II: Sorted Input
desc: `numbers` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the **1-based** indices `[i, j]` (`i < j`) of the two numbers that add up to `target`.
Use only constant extra space.
hints: If the current sum is too small, which pointer should move?
Start with `lo = 0`, `hi = len - 1`.
editorial: Because the array is sorted, a sum that's too small can only grow by moving `lo` right, and a sum too big can only shrink by moving `hi` left. Each step eliminates one element, so it's O(n).

problems.title: 3Sum
desc: Return all **unique** triplets `[a, b, c]` from `nums` (using three different positions) such that `a + b + c == 0`.
The order of triplets and of numbers inside a triplet doesn't matter, but the same triplet must not appear twice.
hints: Sort first. Fix the first number, then it's Two Sum II on the rest.
Skip a value equal to the previous one at every level to avoid duplicates.
editorial: Sort. For each index `i` (skipping repeats of `nums[i]`), run two pointers on `i+1..n-1` looking for `-nums[i]`. After a hit, advance both pointers past equal values. Total O(n²), which beats the O(n³) brute force.
problems.complexity: O(n²) time, O(1) extra space besides the output (sorting aside).

problems.title: Container With Most Water
desc: `height[i]` is the height of a vertical line at position `i`. Choose two lines that, together with the x-axis, hold the most water. Return that maximum area.
Area = (distance between the lines) × (height of the shorter line).
hints: Start with the widest container. Moving the taller line inward can never help. Why?
Always move the shorter line.
editorial: Start with pointers at both ends. The area is limited by the shorter line; moving the taller one can only shrink the width without raising that limit. So move the shorter line each step, tracking the best area.

problems.title: Reverse Words in a String
desc: Return the words of `s` in reverse order, separated by single spaces, with no leading or trailing spaces.
constraints: s contains at least one word
hints: Split into words (ignoring extra spaces), reverse the list, join with single spaces.
Without built-ins: reverse the whole string, then reverse each word.
editorial: Splitting on whitespace discards the extra spaces; reversing the word list and joining with one space gives the answer. The in-place version (for mutable character arrays) reverses the whole string and then each word.

solution.py:
def reverse_words(s):
    return " ".join(reversed(s.split()))

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
desc: `height` describes an elevation map where each bar has width 1. Compute how many units of rain water it traps.
hints: Water above bar i = min(tallest bar to its left, tallest to its right) − height[i].
Two pointers: whichever side has the smaller max is the one whose water level you know for sure.
editorial: Keep `left_max` and `right_max`. If `left_max <= right_max`, the water at `lo` is decided by `left_max` (there's something at least as tall on the right), so add `left_max - height[lo]` and move `lo`. Otherwise do the mirror step on `hi`.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
desc: `prices[i]` is a stock's price on day `i`. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.
hints: For each day as the selling day, what's the best buying day?
Track the cheapest price seen so far.
editorial: One pass: keep the minimum price so far and the best `price - minimum`. Selling today is only worth comparing against the cheapest earlier day.

problems.title: Maximum Average Subarray
desc: Return the maximum average of any contiguous subarray of length exactly `k`.
hints: Compute the first window's sum, then slide.
Sliding: add the new element, subtract the one leaving.
editorial: A fixed-size window: maintain its sum in O(1) per step by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one. Track the best sum and divide by `k` once at the end.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
desc: Return the length of the longest substring of `s` that contains no repeated characters.
hints: Grow a window to the right; when a character repeats, the left edge must jump past its previous occurrence.
Store each character's last index in a dict.
editorial: Keep `left` and a map `last[ch]`. When `s[right]` was seen at an index ≥ `left`, move `left` to that index + 1. The window `s[left..right]` is always repeat-free; track its maximum length.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
desc: You may change up to `k` characters of the uppercase string `s` to any other uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest substring that can be made of one repeated letter.
hints: A window is fixable if (window length − count of its most common letter) ≤ k.
You never need to shrink the best count you've seen; the window just stops growing.
editorial: Slide a window, counting letters and tracking the highest single-letter count `top`. If `size - top > k`, move `left` forward by one. The window never shrinks below the best size found, which is exactly the answer.

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
desc: Given positive integers `nums` and a `target`, return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is **at least** `target`, or 0 if none exists.
hints: All numbers are positive, so growing a window only increases its sum.
Grow on the right; while the sum is ≥ target, record the length and shrink from the left.
editorial: Variable-size window: extend `right`, and while the window sum reaches the target, record its length and drop elements from the left. Positivity guarantees shrinking can only lower the sum, which is what makes this O(n).

problems.title: Permutation in String

problems.title: Last Stone Weight
desc: Each turn, smash the two heaviest stones `x <= y` together. If equal, both are destroyed; otherwise the lighter is destroyed and the heavier becomes `y - x`.
Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.
hints: You repeatedly need the two largest: a max-heap.
In Python, push negated weights into `heapq`.
editorial: Simulate with a max-heap: pop two, push the difference if non-zero, repeat until at most one stone remains.
problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
desc: Design a class that tracks the `k`-th largest score in a stream.
`KthLargest(k, nums)` starts with the scores in `nums`. `add(val)` adds a score and returns the current `k`-th largest. There will always be at least `k` scores when you are asked.
hints: Keep only the k largest scores you've seen; the smallest of them is the answer.
A min-heap of size k does exactly that: push, and pop if it grows past k.
editorial: Hold a min-heap of at most k values. Every add pushes, then pops the minimum if the heap is larger than k. The heap's root is the k-th largest so far.
problems.complexity: O(log k) per add, O(k) space.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
desc: Return the `k`-th largest element of `nums` (in sorted order, not the k-th distinct).
hints: Sorting works in O(n log n). Can you do O(n log k)?
Keep a min-heap of the k largest seen; its root is the answer.
editorial: Push each number onto a min-heap and pop whenever it exceeds size k. The heap always holds the k largest so far, and its smallest element is the k-th largest. Quickselect gives O(n) average.
problems.complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

problems.title: K Closest Points to Origin
desc: Return the `k` points from `points` closest to the origin `(0, 0)` by Euclidean distance, in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique.
hints: Compare squared distances; the square root doesn't change the order.
Sort by `x*x + y*y`, or keep a max-heap of size k.
editorial: Sort by squared distance and take the first k (O(n log n)), or keep a max-heap of size k (O(n log k)).
problems.complexity: O(n log k) time with a heap, O(k) space.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
desc: A CPU runs `tasks` (letters), one per time unit. Two runs of the same letter must be at least `n` units apart, so the CPU may need to sit idle. Return the fewest time units needed to finish every task.
hints: The most frequent task decides the shape: it needs `max_count - 1` gaps of `n` slots after its runs.
Count how many tasks tie for the maximum: they all fit in the final row. If there are more tasks than slots, there's no idling at all.
editorial: Let m be the highest count and t the number of letters with that count. Lay out m rows of width n + 1; the last row only holds the t most frequent letters, giving `(m - 1) × (n + 1) + t`. Other letters fill the idle slots, and if they overflow, the answer is simply the number of tasks. A max-heap simulation gives the same result more slowly.

problems.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
desc: You get `lists`, an array of `k` arrays each sorted in ascending order. Merge them into one sorted array.
The heap version is the point: always take the smallest current front among the k lists.
hints: Put the first item of every list in a min-heap, tagged with which list and index it came from.
Pop the smallest, append it, and push the next item from the same list.
editorial: A heap of k fronts gives the next smallest in O(log k), so N total items take O(N log k). Merging the lists pairwise, like merge sort, has the same cost.
problems.complexity: O(N log k) time, O(k) extra space.

solution.py:
import heapq

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    out = []
    while heap:
        val, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(val)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return out

problems.title: Subsets
desc: Given distinct integers `nums`, return every possible subset (the power set). The order of subsets and of numbers within a subset doesn't matter.
hints: Each element is either in or out: 2ⁿ subsets.
Backtrack: at index i, recurse once without nums[i] and once with it.
editorial: Recursive include/exclude over the indices, or iteratively: start with `[[]]` and for each number add a copy of every existing subset with that number appended.

problems.title: Permutations
desc: Return all permutations of the distinct integers in `nums`, in any order.
hints: Choose an unused number for the next position, recurse, then un-choose it.
Track used numbers with a set or boolean array.
editorial: Classic backtracking: the path grows one number at a time from the unused ones; when its length equals n, record a copy. There are n! permutations.

problems.title: Combination Sum
desc: Given distinct positive `candidates` and a `target`, return all unique combinations whose numbers sum to `target`. Each candidate may be used any number of times.
Two combinations are the same if they use the same numbers the same number of times, regardless of order.
hints: To avoid duplicates like [2,3,2] vs [2,2,3], only allow choosing candidates at index ≥ the last one you chose.
Stop exploring when the remaining target goes negative.
editorial: Backtrack with a start index: at each step try `candidates[i]` for `i >= start`, staying at `i` (reuse allowed). Sorting first lets you break early once a candidate exceeds the remainder.
problems.complexity: Exponential in target / min(candidates) in the worst case.

problems.title: Generate Parentheses
desc: Return every string of `n` pairs of well-formed parentheses, in any order.
hints: You can add '(' while you've used fewer than n.
You can add ')' only while there are more '(' than ')' so far.
editorial: Backtrack on the string being built, tracking opens and closes. The two rules guarantee every completed string is valid, so no filtering is needed. The count is the n-th Catalan number.
problems.complexity: O(Cₙ · n) where Cₙ is the n-th Catalan number.

problems.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
desc: Each digit 2-9 on a phone keypad maps to letters (2 → abc, 3 → def, 4 → ghi, 5 → jkl, 6 → mno, 7 → pqrs, 8 → tuv, 9 → wxyz). Return every string the `digits` could spell, in any order. An empty input gives an empty list.
hints: Build the string one digit at a time; each digit offers 3 or 4 choices.
Recurse with the current prefix and the index of the next digit. When the prefix is as long as `digits`, record it.
editorial: Classic backtracking over a fixed number of positions. Alternatively, start from `[""]` and for each digit replace the list with every string extended by every letter for that digit.
problems.complexity: O(4^n × n) time for n digits.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning
desc: Split `s` into pieces so that every piece is a palindrome. Return every possible split, in any order. Each split lists its pieces left to right.
hints: Choose the first piece: try every prefix that is a palindrome, then split the rest the same way.
When the start index reaches the end of the string, the current list of pieces is one answer.
editorial: Backtrack over the start position. For each end position where `s[start:end]` reads the same backwards, add it to the path, recurse from `end`, then remove it.
problems.complexity: O(n × 2^n) time in the worst case (all letters equal).

problems.title: Word Search
desc: Given a grid of letters `board` and a `word`, return `true` if the word can be traced through the grid.
Each next letter must be in a cell next to the previous one (up, down, left or right), and a cell can't be used twice in one word.
hints: Start a search from every cell that matches the first letter.
Mark a cell as used before recursing into its neighbours, and unmark it afterwards so other paths can use it.
editorial: DFS from each cell with the index of the next letter to match. Temporarily overwrite the cell with a marker while it's on the path, then restore it. Return as soon as the whole word is matched.
problems.complexity: O(rows × cols × 3^L) time for a word of length L.

problems.title: N-Queens: Count Solutions
desc: Place `n` chess queens on an `n × n` board so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal). Return how many distinct arrangements exist.
hints: Place one queen per row; for each row try every column that's safe.
A cell (r, c) is on diagonal r − c and anti-diagonal r + c. Keep sets of used columns and diagonals.
editorial: Backtrack row by row with three sets: used columns, used `r - c` diagonals and used `r + c` anti-diagonals. Each check is O(1), so pruning is cheap and the search finishes instantly for n ≤ 9.
problems.complexity: Roughly O(n!) in the worst case, far less with pruning.

problems.title: Flood Fill
desc: Starting from pixel `(sr, sc)` in `image`, recolour it and every pixel connected to it (up/down/left/right) that has the same original colour, using `color`. Return the image.
hints: If the start pixel already has the new colour, return immediately, or you'll loop forever.
DFS from the start; only spread into pixels of the original colour.
editorial: Remember the original colour; if it equals the new one, nothing changes. Otherwise DFS/BFS recolouring every reachable pixel of the original colour.

problems.title: Number of Islands
desc: `grid` is a 2D map of `"1"` (land) and `"0"` (water). An island is land connected horizontally or vertically. Return the number of islands.
hints: Scan every cell. When you find unvisited land, that's a new island: count it, then sink all its connected land.
Use BFS with a queue to avoid deep recursion on big islands.
editorial: For each land cell, increment the count and flood-fill (BFS/DFS) to mark its whole island as visited. Every cell is processed a constant number of times.

problems.title: Course Schedule
desc: There are `num_courses` courses labelled `0` to `num_courses - 1`. Each pair `[a, b]` in `prerequisites` means you must take `b` before `a`.
Return `true` if you can finish every course (that is, the prerequisites contain no cycle).
hints: Courses are nodes, prerequisites are directed edges. You need to detect a cycle.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a course with no remaining prerequisites.
editorial: Compute in-degrees. Queue all courses with in-degree 0; pop one, 'take' it and decrement the in-degree of courses that depend on it. If you take every course, there's no cycle.

solution.py:
from collections import deque

def can_finish(num_courses, prerequisites):
    after = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    indeg = [0] * num_courses
    for a, b in prerequisites:
        after[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if indeg[i] == 0)
    taken = 0
    while q:
        c = q.popleft()
        taken += 1
        for nxt in after[c]:
            indeg[nxt] -= 1
            if indeg[nxt] == 0:
                q.append(nxt)
    return taken == num_courses

problems.title: Rotting Oranges
desc: In `grid`, 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange and 2 is a rotten orange. Every minute, fresh oranges next to a rotten one (up/down/left/right) become rotten.
Return the minutes until no fresh orange remains, or `-1` if that's impossible.
hints: Multi-source BFS: start the queue with every rotten orange at minute 0.
Count fresh oranges; if any remain after BFS, return -1.
editorial: Seed a BFS queue with all rotten oranges. Process the queue level by level; each level is one minute. Track the fresh count; when it hits zero, the number of levels processed is the answer.

problems.title: Max Area of Island
desc: `grid` holds 1 for land and 0 for water. An island is land cells joined up, down, left or right. Return the area (number of cells) of the largest island, or 0 if there is none.
hints: Same as counting islands, but each flood fill returns the size of what it filled.
Sink each visited cell (set it to 0) so it's never counted twice.
editorial: Scan every cell. At unvisited land, run a DFS or BFS that marks cells as it goes and counts them. Keep the largest count.

problems.title: Number of Provinces
desc: There are `n` cities. `is_connected[i][j]` is 1 if city i and city j are directly linked. A province is a group of cities linked directly or through other cities. Return the number of provinces.
hints: It's the number of connected components in a graph given as an adjacency matrix.
Union-find: union every linked pair, then count distinct roots. Or DFS from every unvisited city.
editorial: Union-find with path compression joins each pair (i, j) with a 1. Every successful union reduces the component count by one, starting from n.

problems.title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
desc: In an n × n `grid` of 0s (open) and 1s (blocked), find the shortest clear path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. You may move in all 8 directions. Return the number of cells on the path, or -1 if there is no path.
hints: Fewest steps in an unweighted grid means BFS.
Check both corners first. Each cell has up to 8 neighbours; mark a cell as visited when you add it to the queue.
editorial: BFS from (0, 0) with distance 1, exploring all 8 neighbours. The first time the bottom-right cell is dequeued, its distance is the answer. If the queue empties first, return -1.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
desc: A network has `n` nodes labelled 1 to n. `times[i] = [u, v, w]` means a signal takes `w` time to travel from u to v (one way). A signal is sent from node `k`. Return how long it takes for every node to receive it, or -1 if some node never does.
hints: It's the longest of the shortest paths from k. Weighted shortest paths call for Dijkstra's algorithm.
Use a min-heap of (time, node). The first time you pop a node, that's its final time.
editorial: Dijkstra from k: pop the closest unsettled node, settle it, and relax its outgoing edges. When the heap is empty, if all n nodes were settled the answer is the largest settled time, otherwise -1.
problems.complexity: O(E log V) time, O(V + E) space.

problems.title: Is Graph Bipartite?
desc: `graph[i]` lists the neighbours of node i in an undirected graph (which may be disconnected). Return `true` if the nodes can be split into two groups so that every edge joins nodes from different groups.
constraints: If v is in graph[u], u is in graph[v]
hints: Try to colour the graph with two colours so neighbours always differ.
BFS from every uncoloured node. If you ever find a neighbour with your own colour, it's not bipartite.
editorial: Two-colouring by BFS or DFS. Start each component with colour 0; give each neighbour the opposite colour. A conflict means an odd cycle, which can't be split into two groups.

problems.title: Word Ladder
desc: Transform `begin_word` into `end_word` by changing one letter at a time; every intermediate word must be in `word_list`.
Return the number of words in the shortest such sequence (including both ends), or 0 if no sequence exists.
constraints: all words have the same length, lowercase letters
hints: Words are nodes; an edge joins words that differ in one letter. Shortest path in an unweighted graph → BFS.
Generate neighbours by replacing each position with a–z and checking a set: O(L × 26) per word.
editorial: BFS from `begin_word`. For each word, try every one-letter change; if the result is in the remaining word set, enqueue it and remove it from the set so it's never revisited. The BFS level at which `end_word` appears is the answer.
problems.complexity: O(N × L × 26) time, O(N × L) space.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
desc: You climb a staircase of `n` steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many distinct ways can you reach the top?
hints: To stand on step n you came from step n−1 or step n−2.
ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2). Look familiar?
editorial: It's the Fibonacci recurrence. Keep only the last two values and iterate; plain recursion without memoisation would be exponential.

problems.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
desc: `cost[i]` is the price of standing on step i. After paying, you can climb one or two steps. You may start on step 0 or step 1. Return the cheapest way to reach the top (just past the last step).
hints: The cheapest way to reach step i comes from step i-1 or step i-2.
You only need the last two answers, not a whole table.
editorial: Let `dp[i]` be the cheapest way to arrive at step i without paying for it yet. You arrive from step i-1 (paying `cost[i-1]`) or from step i-2 (paying `cost[i-2]`), so `dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2])`, with `dp[0] = dp[1] = 0`. The top is step n. Two variables replace the table.

problems.title: House Robber
desc: Houses along a street hold `nums[i]` money. You can't rob two adjacent houses (the alarm links them). Return the most money you can rob.
hints: At house i you either skip it (keep the best up to i−1) or rob it (its money + best up to i−2).
You only need the last two best values.
editorial: `best[i] = max(best[i-1], best[i-2] + nums[i])`. Two rolling variables are enough.

problems.title: Coin Change
desc: Given coin denominations `coins` (unlimited supply of each) and an `amount`, return the fewest coins that make up exactly that amount, or `-1` if it can't be done.
hints: Greedy (always take the biggest coin) fails: try coins [1,3,4] and amount 6.
dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a = 1 + min(dp[a − c]) over coins c.
editorial: Bottom-up DP over amounts 0..amount. `dp[0] = 0`, everything else starts at infinity, and each amount tries every coin. If `dp[amount]` is still infinite, return −1.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
desc: Return the largest sum of any non-empty contiguous subarray of `nums`.
hints: Should the best subarray ending at i extend the one ending at i−1, or start fresh at i?
Start fresh exactly when the running sum has gone negative.
editorial: Kadane's algorithm: `cur = max(x, cur + x)` is the best sum ending here; the answer is the maximum `cur` seen. Initialise with the first element so all-negative arrays work.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
desc: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of `nums` (elements in order, not necessarily adjacent).
hints: O(n²): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
O(n log n): keep `tails[k]` = smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1, and binary search where each number goes.
editorial: Patience sorting: for each number, find the first tail ≥ it (lower bound) and replace it, or append if it's larger than every tail. The number of tails is the LIS length.
problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

problems.title: Unique Paths
desc: A robot starts at the top-left of an `m × n` grid and can only move right or down. How many distinct paths reach the bottom-right corner?
hints: Paths to a cell = paths to the cell above + paths to the cell to the left.
A single row of length n updated m times is enough memory.
editorial: `dp[c] += dp[c-1]` row by row, starting from all ones. (Combinatorics also works: choose which m−1 of the m+n−2 moves go down.)

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
desc: Return the length of the longest subsequence common to `text1` and `text2`, or 0 if there is none.
hints: dp[i][j] = LCS of the first i characters of text1 and the first j of text2.
If the last characters match: 1 + dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]).
editorial: Fill an (n+1) × (m+1) table with the recurrence above. Only the previous row is needed, so memory can drop to O(m).

problems.title: Word Break
desc: Return `true` if `s` can be split into a sequence of one or more words from `word_dict`. Words may be reused.
hints: ok[i] = can the first i characters be segmented?
ok[i] is true if some ok[j] is true and s[j:i] is a word.
editorial: DP over prefix lengths with a set for O(1) word lookups. `ok[0] = True`. For each end `i`, try every start `j` (or only starts within the longest word's length).

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
desc: Return `true` if `nums` can be split into two subsets with equal sums.
hints: If the total is odd, it's impossible. Otherwise: can some subset sum to total / 2?
0/1 knapsack: a set (or boolean array) of reachable sums, updated per number.
editorial: Track all reachable subset sums. For each number, add it to every previously reachable sum. Iterating sums from high to low with a boolean array keeps each number used at most once.

problems.title: Decode Ways
desc: Letters were encoded as numbers: A → 1, B → 2, …, Z → 26. Given a string of digits `s`, return how many ways it could be decoded. A piece with a leading zero, like "06", is not valid.
hints: Like climbing stairs: the last piece uses one digit or two.
One digit is valid if it isn't '0'. Two digits are valid if they form 10 to 26.
editorial: `dp[i]` is the number of ways to decode the first i characters. Add `dp[i-1]` when `s[i-1]` is 1-9, and `dp[i-2]` when `s[i-2:i]` is 10-26. Start with `dp[0] = 1`.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space with two variables.

problems.title: Palindromic Substrings
desc: Return how many substrings of `s` are palindromes. Substrings at different positions count separately, even if they contain the same letters.
hints: Every palindrome has a centre: a single letter or the gap between two letters.
Expand outwards from each of the 2n - 1 centres while the ends match, counting as you go.
editorial: Expand around each centre. For an odd palindrome, start with `lo = hi = i`; for an even one, `lo = i, hi = i + 1`. Each successful expansion is one more palindrome.

problems.title: Maximum Product Subarray
desc: Return the largest product of any non-empty contiguous subarray of `nums`.
constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: A negative number turns the smallest product into the largest.
Track both the largest and the smallest product ending at each position.
editorial: Like Kadane's algorithm, but keep `hi` and `lo`, the max and min products of subarrays ending here. For each x, the candidates are x, hi × x and lo × x; take the max and min of those.

solution.py:
def max_product(nums):
    best = hi = lo = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        cands = (x, hi * x, lo * x)
        hi, lo = max(cands), min(cands)
        best = max(best, hi)
    return best

problems.title: House Robber II
desc: Same as House Robber, except the houses stand in a circle, so the first and last houses are neighbours. Return the most money you can take without taking from two neighbouring houses.
hints: You can't take both the first and the last house. So solve two straight-line problems.
Answer = max(rob(nums without the last), rob(nums without the first)). Handle a single house separately.
editorial: Reuse the linear House Robber DP on `nums[:-1]` and `nums[1:]` and return the larger result. With one house, just take it.

problems.title: Target Sum
desc: Put a `+` or `-` in front of every number in `nums`, then add them all up. Return how many different sign choices give exactly `target`.
hints: Brute force is 2^n. Notice that many sign choices reach the same running total.
Keep a dict from running total to the number of ways to reach it, and update it for each number.
editorial: Process numbers one at a time with `ways[total]`. Each number turns every total t into t + x and t - x, adding up the counts. At the end, return `ways[target]`. (A subset-sum transformation, `(sum + target) / 2`, works too.)
problems.complexity: O(n × S) time, where S is the range of possible sums.

problems.title: Edit Distance
desc: Return the minimum number of single-character operations (insert, delete or replace) needed to turn `word1` into `word2`.
hints: dp[i][j] = edits to turn the first i chars of word1 into the first j of word2.
If the last characters match, no edit is needed for them; otherwise 1 + the min of insert, delete or replace.
editorial: Levenshtein DP: base rows `dp[i][0] = i` and `dp[0][j] = j`. Transition: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]` if the characters match, else `1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1])`.
problems.complexity: O(n × m) time, O(m) space with a rolling row.

problems.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
desc: Given a string of `(` and `)`, return the length of the longest substring that is a well-formed (balanced) set of parentheses.
hints: Keep a stack of indexes. Put -1 on it first as a 'last unmatched position' marker.
On `(` push its index. On `)` pop; if the stack is now empty push this index as the new marker, otherwise the valid run is `i - stack[-1]` long.
editorial: The bottom of the stack is always the index just before the current valid run. Every time a `)` matches, the run ends at i and starts after the index now on top. A DP over 'longest valid ending at i' also works in O(n).

problems.title: Merge Intervals
desc: Merge all overlapping intervals in `intervals` (each `[start, end]`) and return the non-overlapping result, sorted by start. Touching intervals like `[1,4]` and `[4,5]` overlap.
hints: Sort by start. Then an interval overlaps the previous merged one exactly when its start ≤ the previous end.
Extend the previous end with max(), don't overwrite it.
editorial: Sort by start. Keep a result list; if the next interval starts at or before the last result's end, extend that end to the maximum; otherwise append it.
problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

problems.title: Insert Interval
desc: `intervals` is sorted by start and non-overlapping. Insert `new_interval` and merge where necessary. Return the resulting sorted, non-overlapping list.
hints: Three phases: intervals entirely before, overlapping, entirely after.
While overlapping, grow the new interval to cover each one.
editorial: Copy intervals ending before the new one starts; then merge every interval whose start ≤ the new end into it; then copy the rest. One linear pass.

problems.title: Jump Game
desc: You start at index 0. `nums[i]` is the maximum jump length from index `i`. Return `true` if you can reach the last index.
hints: Track the farthest index reachable so far.
If you ever stand at an index beyond the farthest reach, you're stuck.
editorial: Scan left to right keeping `reach = max(reach, i + nums[i])`. If `i > reach` at any point, return false. Greedy works because reachability is just an interval [0, reach].

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
desc: Return the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest don't overlap. Intervals that only touch (like `[1,2]` and `[2,3]`) do not overlap.
hints: Keep as many as possible instead: the classic activity-selection problem.
Sort by end time; always keep the interval that finishes first.
editorial: Sort by end. Keep an interval if it starts at or after the end of the last kept one; otherwise remove it. Choosing the earliest finish leaves the most room for the rest (exchange argument).
problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Gas Station
desc: Stations are arranged in a circle. Station `i` gives `gas[i]` fuel, and driving to station `i + 1` costs `cost[i]`. With an empty tank, from which station index can you drive all the way around once? Return it, or `-1`. The answer is unique if it exists.
hints: If total gas < total cost, it's impossible.
If you run dry going from start to i, no station between start and i can be the answer either; restart at i + 1.
editorial: One pass tracking the tank since the current candidate start. When the tank drops below zero at i, set start = i + 1 and reset the tank. If the overall sum of gas − cost is non-negative, the final start works.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
desc: `intervals[i] = [start, end]` is a meeting from `start` up to (not including) `end`. Return the fewest rooms needed so no two meetings in the same room overlap. A meeting ending at 10 frees its room for one starting at 10.
hints: The answer is the most meetings happening at the same moment.
Sort the start times and the end times separately. Sweep through starts; each start that comes before the earliest unused end needs a new room.
editorial: Sort starts and ends. Walk the starts with pointer i and the ends with pointer j. If `starts[i] < ends[j]`, a new room is needed; otherwise a meeting ended, so reuse its room and advance j. A min-heap of end times gives the same answer.
problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

problems.title: Jump Game II
desc: You start at index 0. `nums[i]` is the farthest you can jump forward from index i. Return the fewest jumps needed to reach the last index. You can always reach it.
hints: Think in layers, like BFS: every index reachable with j jumps forms a range.
Track the end of the current layer and the farthest point the next layer reaches. When you pass the end, take a jump.
editorial: Scan left to right keeping `end` (the edge of what's reachable with the current number of jumps) and `far` (the edge for one more jump). When i reaches `end`, add a jump and set `end = far`. Stop before the last index.

problems.title: Partition Labels
desc: Split `s` into as many pieces as possible so that each letter appears in at most one piece. Return the sizes of the pieces, left to right.
hints: Record the last position of every letter.
Grow the current piece until its end reaches the last position of every letter inside it; then cut.
editorial: First pass: `last[c]` for each letter. Second pass: extend `end = max(end, last[s[i]])`; when `i == end`, the piece from `start` to `end` is complete.

problems.title: Single Number
desc: Every element of `nums` appears twice except one. Return that one, using O(1) extra memory.
hints: What is x XOR x? What is x XOR 0?
XOR is commutative, so order doesn't matter.
editorial: XOR all numbers together. Pairs cancel to 0 and the lone number remains.

problems.title: Missing Number
desc: `nums` contains `n` distinct numbers from the range `[0, n]`. Return the one number in that range that is missing.
hints: The sum 0 + 1 + … + n is n(n+1)/2.
Subtract the actual sum.
editorial: Expected sum minus actual sum. (XOR-ing every index and value also works and never overflows in fixed-width languages.)

problems.title: Counting Bits
desc: For every `i` from 0 to `n`, count the 1-bits in its binary form. Return the list of counts.
Try for O(n) without counting each number from scratch.
hints: `i >> 1` is i with its last bit removed, and you already know its count.
bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
editorial: DP on the binary representation: shifting right drops the lowest bit, so `bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output.

problems.title: Power of Two
desc: Return `true` if `n` is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …).
hints: A power of two has exactly one 1-bit.
`n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest 1-bit.
editorial: Positive and `n & (n - 1) == 0`. Zero and negatives are never powers of two.

solution.py:
def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0

problems.title: Hamming Distance
desc: The Hamming distance between two numbers is how many bit positions differ. Return it for `x` and `y`.
hints: `x ^ y` has a 1 exactly where the bits differ.
Count the 1 bits: `n & (n - 1)` removes the lowest one.
editorial: XOR the numbers, then count set bits. Each `n &= n - 1` clears one, so the loop runs once per differing bit.

problems.title: Reverse Bits
desc: Treat `n` as a 32-bit unsigned integer. Reverse the order of its 32 bits and return the result as an unsigned integer.
hints: Take bits off the bottom of n one at a time and push them onto the bottom of the result.
Do it exactly 32 times, so leading zeros become trailing zeros. In JavaScript, `>>> 0` (or multiplying by 2 instead of `<<`) keeps results unsigned.
editorial: Loop 32 times: `result = result * 2 + (n & 1)`, then shift n right by one. Using multiplication instead of `<<` avoids JavaScript's signed 32-bit overflow.

problems.title: Min Stack
desc: Design a stack that supports `push(val)`, `pop()`, `top()` and `get_min()` (JavaScript: `getMin()`), each in O(1) time.
The tests call your methods in sequence. `pop`, `top` and `get_min` are only called on a non-empty stack.
hints: Store, alongside each value, the minimum of the stack at the moment it was pushed.
Or keep a second stack of minimums.
editorial: Push pairs `(val, min_so_far)`, where `min_so_far = min(val, previous min)`. The top pair always knows the current minimum, so every operation is O(1).

problems.title: LRU Cache
desc: Design a Least Recently Used cache with a fixed `capacity`.

`get(key)` returns the value, or `-1` if absent. `put(key, value)` inserts or updates; if that exceeds the capacity, evict the least recently used key. Both must run in O(1) average time. Reading or writing a key makes it the most recently used.
hints: A dict gives O(1) lookup; you also need O(1) 'move to most recent' and 'drop least recent'.
Python's `OrderedDict` has `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)`. A JavaScript `Map` remembers insertion order, so delete and re-insert to refresh.
editorial: Pair a hash map with an ordering structure. With an ordered map: on get, move the key to the end; on put, update/insert at the end and pop from the front when over capacity. The classic hand-built version uses a doubly linked list plus a dict of nodes.
problems.complexity: O(1) average per operation, O(capacity) space.

problems.title: Time Based Key-Value Store
desc: Store several values for the same key at different timestamps.

`set(key, value, timestamp)` stores a value. `get(key, timestamp)` returns the value set with the largest timestamp `<=` the given one, or `""` if there is none. Timestamps for `set` arrive in strictly increasing order.
hints: A dict from key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs. Because timestamps only grow, each list stays sorted.
`get` is a binary search for the last timestamp that is `<=` the one asked for.
editorial: Append on `set`. On `get`, binary search the key's list for the rightmost timestamp not after the query. Python's `bisect_right` does this in one call.

problems.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
desc: A trie stores words letter by letter in a tree, so words that share a prefix share a path.
`insert(word)` adds a word. `search(word)` returns `true` if that exact word was inserted. `starts_with(prefix)` (`startsWith` in JavaScript) returns `true` if any inserted word begins with `prefix`.
hints: Each node is a dict from letter to child node, plus a flag saying whether a word ends here.
`search` and `starts_with` both walk the path; they only differ in whether the final node must be marked as a word end.
editorial: Write one helper that follows a string from the root and returns the last node (or nothing if the path breaks). `search` checks that node's end flag; `starts_with` only checks that it exists. `insert` walks the same way, creating nodes as needed.
problems.complexity: O(L) per operation for a word of length L.
